newsitem.title: USA: U.S., UK in new talks to forge 'open skies' pact.
newsitem.headline: U.S., UK in new talks to forge 'open skies' pact.

text.p: The United States and Britain are to make yet another attempt on Wednesday to reach an "open skies" aviation accord that would end restrictions on airline traffic between the two countries.
Past efforts have all ended in failure, the most recent in August when the United States cancelled talks then under way, citing lack of progress.
The resumed effort was requested by Washington.
U.S. officials called the talks on Wednesday and Thursday preliminary and said they would enter a "negotiations" stage, later this month, in London, only if progress was made.
The busy U.S.-British air link is now heavily regulated.

Airline access to London's Heathrow airport has been a sticking point in previous talks to end restrictions and the U.S. officials made it clear that expanded Heathrow landing rights had to be part of any new bilateral aviation accord.

British Airways Plc. controls 38 percent of landing slots at Heathrow -- considered a vital transfer point for service beyond to continental Europe -- but has been reluctant to cede them to its U.S. transatlantic competitors.
And the United States has said an "open skies" accord could not be reached without an opening of Heathrow.

Referring to Heathrow, an official said "the U.S. goal remains acceptance of all essential elements of an 'open skies' regime in an operating environment that allows the available rights to be exercised effectively."

While BA has been protective of its Heathrow slots, it and the big U.S. carrier American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp., need an "open skies" accord if the U.S. Government is to approve their planned transatlantic alliance.
U.S. officials have said government immunity from antitrust laws would not be granted American Airlines unless an "open skies" accord was first reached.
"Open skies" would give U.S. and British carriers the right to fly into any city in the other's country as often as they wish. Routes and frequencies are now tightly controlled.
U.S. carriers with foreign marketing alliances include United Airlines, a unit of UAL Corp., with Deutsche Lufthansa AG, and Northwest Airlines, with KLM Royal Dutch Airlines NV.
But those alliances, and antitrust immunity, followed U.S. free-market aviation accords with Germany and the Netherlands.
U.S. officials gave no reason for initiating the new set of talks, but said the United States had remained in touch with the British since the last round of talks was called off.
The talks this week would be "government-to-government," they said, with no industry representatives at the table.
But, they added, if progress was made and negotiations opened later this month, the industry would be brought in for its views on a new U.S.-British aviation arrangement.
